audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Friday, June nineteenth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters as you head into the weekend.

Let's start with marketing and AI, because two stories landed this week that speak directly to the consulting practice you're building — and together they paint a very clear picture of where the market is heading.

The first is from Think with Google, and it's framed as a guide for CMOs on how to rewire their teams around AI. The core argument is this: most organisations are treating AI as a tool you bolt onto an existing structure — a new platform, a new vendor, maybe a new hire. Google's thesis is that that's insufficient. Real AI transformation in a marketing function requires rethinking the team architecture itself: what roles exist, what skills are valued, how work flows from insight to execution. That's a significant reframe, and it's exactly the kind of reframe that creates consulting opportunity. Because that kind of structural change is uncomfortable, it's politically difficult inside an organisation, and it almost always benefits from an external voice who can name the problem and model what the new state looks like. If you're building proposals for Canadian institutional or corporate clients, the Google framework gives you a credible intellectual backbone to anchor the conversation.

The second story is Adobe and LinkedIn jointly announcing a global learning initiative explicitly designed to close the marketing AI skills gap. Think about what that signals: two of the largest platforms that marketers live inside every day have concluded that the gap is real, significant, and worth a co-investment to address at scale. That's not a niche problem anymore — that's infrastructure being built to address a mass deficit. For you, this is both a signal and a potential positioning tool. It validates your thesis. And practically speaking, these programmes will credential tens of thousands of marketers — but they won't replace the senior strategic guidance that helps an organisation actually apply those skills to its specific brand, its specific audience, its specific moment. That's the irreplaceable layer, and that's where you sit.

On the more creative side of marketing, Adweek this week rounded up the standout World Cup ad campaigns, and the clear winner pattern is brands that leaned into hyper-local cultural codes rather than generic global messaging. Adidas backing Scotland, Brahma tapping into Brazilian football mythology — the campaigns that are cutting through are doing so because they feel specific and rooted rather than polished and universal. There's a lesson there that travels well into any brand strategy conversation, particularly with clients who are tempted to over-generalise their positioning in the name of reach. Relevance beats reach. Every time.

Now into higher education, where there's a lot moving this week and several stories that land close to home.

The most strategically interesting piece comes from ICEF Monitor, which published a summary of a whitepaper based on two thousand five hundred student conversations about study-abroad decisions. The finding is striking: the decisive variable in whether a student who has already received an offer actually enrols is not the quality of the offer itself, or the ranking of the institution, or even the financial package. It's emotional uncertainty in the window between receiving the offer and making the final decision. Students who feel anxious, unsupported, or confused during that period are the ones who drop out of the funnel — often silently, without giving the institution any feedback that would let them course-correct.

Here's why this matters for you specifically: that gap is a marketing and customer experience problem, not an admissions operations problem. The fix isn't more information — it's better reassurance, delivered in the right format, through the right channel, at the right emotional moment. That is a brief you could walk into any Canadian university international recruitment office and pitch directly. The whitepaper gives you the evidence base, and your background in brand strategy and AI-driven personalisation gives you the delivery mechanism. This is a strong consulting pitch waiting to happen.

Closer to home, Royal Roads University and BCIT have announced a formal partnership to give students faster, more flexible, and more affordable pathways to credentials. On its face this is an enrolment strategy story — both institutions are trying to compete on value as domestic and international student numbers face pressure. But announcements like this almost always generate downstream work: how do you market the new pathway? How do you communicate brand alignment between two institutions with distinct identities? How do you reach prospective students who didn't previously see either institution as an option? That's a marketing strategy brief, and if you have or want a relationship with either RRU or BCIT, this is a good moment to make contact.

Also worth flagging: Thompson Rivers University — your local institution in Kamloops — is navigating a vote by support workers on a tentative labour deal, set against a backdrop of budget cuts and what's being described as low morale on campus. Labour disputes and budget pressure together are a classic indicator of institutional stress, and stressed institutions sometimes become receptive to external expertise they might not have sought in calmer conditions. Keep an eye on how TRU leadership navigates the coming weeks.

On the global side of international student flows, there are two signals pulling in opposite directions for Canada. First, the White House has finalised a regulation that gives international students in the United States more flexibility around programme changes and duration of stay — making the US a comparatively more attractive destination at a moment when Canada has been tightening its own policies. Second, Türkiye is continuing its extraordinary rise as an alternative study destination, drawing students from Asia, Africa, and the Middle East who are priced out of traditional English-speaking markets. Canada is losing competitive ground on multiple fronts simultaneously. For anyone advising Canadian institutions on international recruitment strategy, the framing of this moment matters: the window to differentiate and retain international student interest is now, before more students route permanently to alternative destinations.

On the pure AI and technology front, three stories worth your attention today.

MIT Technology Review is covering a Miami-based startup called Subquadratic, which came out of stealth last month with a bold claim: it has solved a mathematical bottleneck in how large language models process information — a constraint that has apparently been limiting LLM performance for close to a decade. The reception was sceptical when the claim was first made, understandably so. But the company is now beginning to share technical evidence, and MIT Tech Review is treating it as a story worth watching. If the claim holds up under scrutiny, this would be a meaningful step-change in LLM capability — not an incremental improvement but a structural one. Worth bookmarking and revisiting as more independent analysis comes in.

Also from MIT Technology Review: brain-computer interface trials are accelerating, and the milestone story this week is Casey Harrell, a man living with ALS who has been using a brain implant for nearly three years and is described by his research team as the technology's first genuine power user. He can communicate and interact with digital systems despite being paralysed and unable to speak clearly without the device. The reason this belongs in your briefing isn't the technology per se — it's the pace signal. BCI trials are scaling up, the clinical evidence base is deepening, and the gap between experimental and applied is closing faster than most people expected five years ago. As an AI-focused executive, understanding where the human-machine interface is heading is part of your intellectual territory.

The third story: the US government and ASML are in a public dispute over whether China has obtained ASML's most advanced chip-making tool — the kind of EUV machine that is essential for producing the most cutting-edge semiconductors and that is subject to strict export controls. ASML says China does not have it. Washington says it may. The fact that this dispute is happening in public is itself significant — it suggests the controls may be less airtight than assumed, and it adds another layer of uncertainty to global semiconductor supply chains at a moment when AI hardware demand is putting intense pressure on production capacity.

On real estate, one story worth a read this morning. HousingWire has a piece on the growing trend of aging in place — the shift among older homeowners toward staying in their current homes rather than downsizing or moving to assisted-living facilities. The article notes that what was once a lifestyle preference is increasingly becoming a financial decision: in many markets, selling a long-held property and trying to buy or rent something more suitable is simply too expensive. The implication is a widening gap between housing stock and the needs of an aging population, with renovation and modification demand rising as a result.

For you this is relevant on a few levels. You hold property in Sun Peaks, Langley, and Vancouver — three markets where this dynamic plays out differently but is present in all of them. And as someone who tracks the real estate industry closely, including brokerage trends, the aging-in-place shift also changes what buyers and sellers look like, what inventory looks like, and what agents need to be communicating to clients navigating these decisions. It's a slow-moving structural trend, but the smart money is paying attention now.

Locally in Kamloops and Sun Peaks, three things caught my attention this morning.

TRU's labour situation I've already covered in the higher-ed context, but it's worth naming here too because it affects the day-to-day feel of the institution — the people who run front-line student services are the support workers involved in this vote, and how this resolves will shape TRU's ability to deliver on its student experience promises heading into fall enrolment.

At Sun Peaks, the community is gathering this week for its second annual Summersgiving meal — a community event that on its surface is just a nice local story, but which reflects something real: Sun Peaks is developing an increasingly confident year-round residential identity, separate from and beyond its ski resort brand. That transition matters for property values, for local services, and for how the community positions itself to future residents and investors.

And at the Federation of Canadian Municipalities meeting, a Kamloops councillor returned with infrastructure funding and homelessness identified as the city's defining challenges. Neither is new — but the FCM platform means Kamloops is actively seeking federal and provincial engagement on both issues. For anyone with a long-term stake in Kamloops-area property, these are the policy levers that will shape liveability and investment attractiveness over the next decade.

Globally, two stories that a senior executive should have on their radar heading into the weekend.

President Trump gave an interview to Axios in which he stated he has discovered, quote, no limits to his power since going to war with Iran. A forthcoming book, according to the report, reveals him entertaining the idea that he may be the most powerful person in history, placing himself in the lineage of conquerors and strongmen. This is not partisan commentary — it's a factual description of what the sitting US president is saying about his own authority. For Canadian executives and organisations with US exposure, the trajectory of US institutional norms is a material business risk factor, not an abstract political concern. The unpredictability premium on US-dependent strategies is rising.

In Washington D.C., voters have elected a democratic socialist mayor — Janeese Lewis George — decisively defeating a moderate in the primary. She joins New York and Seattle as the latest major US city to make this move, but the analysis worth paying attention to is that her win was driven less by ideological enthusiasm and more by acute anger about the cost of living and housing. The affordability crisis is now consistently producing electoral results that surprise conventional political forecasters. That dynamic is worth understanding, because the policy responses it generates — rent control, development restrictions, anti-corporate housing measures — have real implications for property markets and urban investment across North America.

Finally, one brief cultural note. Today is Juneteenth — the US federal holiday commemorating the end of slavery. Axios has a thoughtful piece noting that the holiday is surviving the corporate DEI retreat, but in a quieter, more internalised form. Companies that made prominent public commitments post-2020 are scaling those back, renaming programmes, or eliminating them entirely — but the holiday itself endures because it's now embedded in payroll systems and federal calendars. For executives managing communications around values and culture, the lesson is worth sitting with: the visibility of a commitment and the durability of a commitment are not the same thing. In a moment when institutional authenticity is being tested from multiple directions, that distinction matters.

That's your Friday briefing, Midya. The through-line this week is institutions under pressure — universities managing budgets and labour, marketing organisations scrambling to build AI capability, governments testing the limits of their authority. The executives who will do well in this environment are the ones who can offer clarity when everything feels uncertain, and that is precisely the value proposition you're building. Have a strong finish to the week, and enjoy the mountain.
